article_text:
東京都美術館で11月14日に開幕する「オルセー美術館所蔵 いまを生きる歓び」でアンバサダーを務める香取慎吾さんが、11月13日に行われたプレス内覧会に登場し、「名作たちの力で、この空間には時間に追われる感覚がない。本当にこのチャンスを逃さないでください」と、来場を呼びかけました。

香取さんはまず、本展を見て回った印象について「とても素敵な時間で、心もなんだか穏やかで、とても幸せです。忙しい毎日を送っていたりしますが、今、見させていただいて本当に心が穏やかです。香取慎吾の状態が、とてもいいです」と笑わせました。

SNSが大好きで、毎日スマートフォンが手放せないという香取さんですが、「久々にどっぷり、たっぷりと自分だけの時間（に浸り）、そして他では見られない素晴らしい作品に囲まれて、『あぁ、こんな時間があったんだな』という、知ってるようで知らない大切な時間を改めて見つけられた気がします」と続け、「自分でもびっくりするぐらいコメントが素晴らしい」と自身の状態の良さを強調しました。

アーティストとしても活躍する香取さんは、美術館で作品がどこから描かれたのかが気になるそうで、「何層にも重なり合っている絵の具を、どこから描いたんだろうとか。筆の運びでも、全体を筆の流れでも表現しているなとか。どこから計算されて出来上がった一枚絵なのかなとか。一つの絵を見ているだけでも時間が足りないぐらい楽しいです」と目を輝かせます。

ミレーの《落穂拾い》でも「前の3人に目が行っていたんですけど、その後ろの方で作業している方がたくさんいて、その右手には馬に乗った方が何か指示を出しているとか、隠されているわけではないんですが、やはり紙やネットで見ているだけでは見えないものがあります」と、実際に美術館に足を運んで見ることの大切さを指摘します。しかも、その作品を見られる距離が「本当に大丈夫ですか？ というぐらい近いんですよ、全部」と話し、自分で個展を開く際には「近すぎないかとすごく気にしていましたが、『何をやってるんだ、俺は』と思いました」と反省を口にしました。

もうひとつの目玉であるゴッホの《星月夜》については、「とても素敵で、息が止まります。ヨーロッパに何度も行くようになって、どうしても持って帰れないのがヨーロッパで見る夜景の素晴らしさです。一応、スマートフォンで写真を撮ったりするんだけど、その時見たその情景は持って帰れていない。だけど、ゴッホの《星月夜》は、『これがいつも僕が見ているもの』です。『いつも見ていて素晴らしい。でも持って帰れない』ものが、今この日本に来て、見られるのは本当に嬉しい瞬間です。（《星月夜が》来日するのは16年ぶりで）本当に見逃せないです」と、言葉に力を込めました。

本展のテーマ「今を生きる喜び」について、香取さんは「まさに今ですね。今もう最高な状態です。忙しくいろんなお仕事させてもらってて、忙しいから疲れちゃう時もあるかもしれないけど、やっぱり人に求めてもらえて動かなきゃいけない、やらなければいけないことがある時間っていうのは幸せだと改めて感じています。特に、こんな風に本当に大好きで憧れの場所で、そこに自分がアンバサダーとして立っていられて、そして自分の言葉によって一人でも多くの人にこの体験をしてほしい、ここに足を運んでほしいということを伝えられる今が、本当に喜びです」と、笑顔を見せました。

ファンへのメッセージとしては「本当にこのチャンスを逃さないでください。僕も今日ここに来させてもらって、本当に心が落ち着いて、穏やかに、自分の中の時間がゆっくり流れる。最近はどんどん時間が早くなってる気がしていて、時間に追われる感覚があるんですけど、この空間にはそれがない。逆にすごいゆったりと時間が進んでいるんで、それはやっぱり名作たちの力が、そうさせてくれるんだと思う。その時間を楽しんでいただいて、オルセー美術館の素晴らしさを自分の中に少しでも取り込んでもらえたら嬉しいです。そして、この東京都美術館の気持ちよさも味わっていただけると、本当に素敵な時間が送れると思います。絶対お勧めなので、みなさんぜひ足を運んでください」と、来場を呼びかけました。

その後、一部メディアを対象に合同インタビューも行われました。ほかに気になっている作品についてうかがうと、カミーユ・カバイヨ＝ラサールの《1874年のサロン》を挙げてくれました。1874年の官展（サロン）に出品された作品です。画中画が６点描かれていますが、すべて実際にサロンに展示された絵です。カバイヨ＝ラサールは、事前にそれぞれの画家のアトリエにカンヴァスを持って行き、それぞれの作家に出品作のミニチュアを描いてもらっていました。

香取さんは「後にこのサロンが開かれた時には、これ（画中画）と同じで大きい作品を、それぞれの作者が書いたものが、ここに飾られたらしいんですね。これは面白いです。この作者がそれぞれの作家の真似をして全部書いたのでも十分なのに、ちゃんとその人の所へ持って行って一個ずつ書いてもらった。ミレーやゴッホの名作以外にも本当に見どころがあります」と話します。

国内外で個展を開くなど、作家としても活躍されている香取さんですが、数々の名作を目の当たりにして制作意欲はかき立てられたのでしょうか。「 今日は自分も絵を描く方なんで、絵をたくさん見て描きたくなったのかというと、実はそっちじゃなくて」と意外な言葉を口にしました。 実はごく最近、依頼を受けて描いた作品があったそうですが、本展を見て色々と考えてしまったそうです。「あまり振り返る方じゃないので、今日はちょっと珍しいです」と続けます。ポスターや会社のロゴ、雑誌の表紙など、依頼を受けた絵にはテーマがあります。それを意識する必要があるものの、以前より自由に描けるようになったと思っていたそうですが、本展の多くの傑作に触れ、まだまだだと感じたそうです。技術だけでなく、作者の遊び心や感覚にも刺激を受け、これらを自分の中で消化し、熟成できた時の作品に期待が膨らみます。（美術展ナビ編集班・若水浩） ◆開幕記事

title_original: Barbara Hepworth Sculpture Sells for $8.3 M., Leading Christie’s London Auction
editorial_title_zh: 芭芭拉·赫普沃斯雕塑以830万美元成交，领跑佳士得伦敦拍卖会
editorial_excerpt_zh: 周三的拍卖使佳士得10月20日和21世纪伦敦拍卖会的总成交额达到了2.786亿英镑（3.714亿美元）。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "周三在伦敦佳士得，芭芭拉·赫普沃斯（Barbara Hepworth）度过了相当不错的一个夜晚。她的三件雕塑作品成为该拍卖行现代英国及爱尔兰艺术晚间拍卖中成交额最高的拍品，其中包括一件打破该英国艺术家单一作品拍卖纪录的作品。", "links": [{"text": "Barbara Hepworth", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/barbara-hepworth/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当晚的明星是创作于1946年的《带色彩的雕塑（厄俄斯）》（Sculpture with Colour (Eos)），成交价为619万英镑（830万美元），在其500万至800万英镑的估价范围内。这件雕塑由一块浅色霍普顿伍德（Hopton Wood）石材整体雕刻而成，其名字取自希腊神话中的黎明女神。（所有拍卖价格均包含买家佣金。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "紧随其后的是另外两件赫普沃斯雕塑。创作于1960年的《人像（苏尼翁）》（Figure (Sunion)）拍得412万英镑（550万美元），而创作于1958年的《海之形（波斯梅尔）》（Sea Form (Porthmeor)）则以154万英镑（210万美元）售出。这两件作品加上前述作品，共计占当晚2310万英镑（3080万美元）总成交额的一半以上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据佳士得称，本次拍卖额比去年同期的同类拍卖会增长了30%，而且创纪录的艺术家不止赫普沃斯一人。沃尔特·西克特（Walter Sickert）的《威尼斯圣马可的马》（The Horses of St Mark’s, Venice）（1901）在经过超过6分钟的竞价后以55.04万英镑（73.4万美元）成交，创下该画家的新拍卖纪录。格鲁克（Gluck）的作品《色调》（Chromatic）（1932）以49.92万英镑（66.5万美元）成交；尤恩·乌格洛（Euan Uglow）的作品《金字塔》（Pyramid）（1993–96）拍得79.36万英镑（106万美元）；爱德华多·保罗齐（Eduardo Paolozzi）的作品《9XSR》（1958）拍得20.48万英镑（27.3万美元），均刷新了各自的拍卖纪录。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "赫普沃斯于1946年创作了《带色彩的雕塑（厄俄斯）》，当时她搬到康沃尔郡已有7年，那里的海岸线、悬崖和古老巨石对其创作产生了重大影响。这座雕塑也是她尝试在雕刻形态中加入色彩的例证，这后来成为了她艺术实践中的一个重要部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年早些时候，这件作品曾在伦敦考陶尔德美术馆（Courtauld Gallery）的“赫普沃斯与色彩”（Hepworth in Colour）展览中亮相，该展览专门聚焦于她艺术生涯中较少为人所知的一面。赫普沃斯1903年出生于约克郡韦克菲尔德，其成年后的很长一段时间都在康沃尔郡圣艾夫斯度过。从1949年直到1975年逝世，她一直在特鲁温工作室（Trewyn Studio）工作。该工作室现在是由泰特美术馆运营的芭芭拉·赫普沃斯博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "周三的拍卖使佳士得10月20日和21世纪伦敦拍卖会的总成交额达到了2.786亿英镑（3.714亿美元），本周晚些时候还将在巴黎举行更多场次的拍卖。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Barbara Hepworth had quite a night at Christie’s in London on Wednesday. Three of her sculptures were the top-selling lots in the auction house’s modern British and Irish art evening sale, including one that set a new record for a unique work by the British artist.

The star of the evening was Sculpture with Colour (Eos) , from 1946, which sold for £6.19 million ($8.3 million), within its £5 million–£8 million estimate. The sculpture, carved from a single block of pale Hopton Wood stone, takes its name from the Greek goddess of dawn. (All sale prices include buyer’s premium.)

Two more Hepworth sculptures followed. Figure (Sunion) , from 1960, brought in £4.12 million ($5.5 million), while Sea Form (Porthmeor) , from 1958, sold for £1.54 million ($2.1 million). Together, the three works accounted for more than half of the evening’s £23.1 million ($30.8 million) total.

The sale was up 30 percent from the equivalent auction last year, according to Christie’s, and Hepworth wasn’t the only artist setting records. Walter Sickert’s The Horses of St Mark’s, Venice (1901) sold for £550,400 ($734,000) after more than six minutes of bidding, setting a new auction record for the painter. New records were also set for Gluck, whose Chromatic (1932) sold for £499,200 ($665,000); Euan Uglow, whose Pyramid (1993–96) fetched £793,600 ($1.06 million); and Eduardo Paolozzi, whose 9XSR (1958) brought in £204,800 ($273,000).

Hepworth made Sculpture with Colour (Eos) in 1946, seven years after moving to Cornwall, where the coastline, cliffs, and ancient stones became a major influence on her work. The sculpture is also an example of her experiments with adding color to carved forms, something that became an important part of her practice.

Earlier this year, the work appeared in “Hepworth in Colour” at London’s Courtauld Gallery, an exhibition devoted to that less familiar side of her career. Born in Wakefield, Yorkshire, in 1903, Hepworth spent much of her adult life in St Ives, Cornwall. She worked from Trewyn Studio from 1949 until her death in 1975. The studio is now the Barbara Hepworth Museum, operated by Tate.

Wednesday’s sale brought Christie’s running total for its October 20th- and 21st-century auctions in London to £278.6 million ($371.4 million), with more sales scheduled in Paris this week.

article_text:
The lean, rugged US actor Tom Skerritt, who has died aged 93, was described by one screenwriter as “a character actor trapped in a leading man’s body”. He took significant roles as authority figures in the films Alien, Top Gun and A River Runs Through It before landing star billing in the 1990s TV family drama Picket Fences, as a sheriff trying to keep the peace in a rural Wisconsin town plagued by violent – and bizarre – crimes.

Skerritt’s breakthrough had come in the 1970 film M*A*S*H , directed by Robert Altman . He played Augustus “Duke” Forrest, a US army surgeon in the Korean war exuding southern charm at the 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital. Along with his fellow surgeons, Benjamin Franklin “Hawkeye” Pierce ( played by Donald Sutherland ) and “Trapper” John McIntyre (Elliott Gould), Duke displayed cynicism and irreverence towards his superiors.

But Skerritt’s character was not transferred to the TV series that followed. While some sources reported that the actor had no faith in the film working as a half-hour sitcom, the writer Larry Gelbart , who adapted the novel for the small screen with Gene Reynolds, explained they wanted characters they felt could generate storylines, adding: “Trapper John just seemed more colourful than Duke.”

Skerritt remained prolific in character roles in films and on TV until coming to worldwide attention as the doomed Captain Dallas, in charge of the commercial space tug Nostromo, in the sci-fi horror movie Alien (1979), which made a star of Sigourney Weaver.

He initially turned down the role, but changed his mind when he heard that it was to be directed by Ridley Scott, whose debut film, the Napoleonic wars drama The Duellists (1977), he regarded as a “classic … a painting from beginning to end”.

Skerritt appeared alongside another actor reaching star status, Tom Cruise, in Top Gun (1986), directed by Ridley’s brother Tony Scott . He played Mike “Viper” Metcalf, mentoring the fighter pilot Pete “Maverick” Mitchell (Cruise) in the elite US navy school.

His own slow-burn rise to stardom was boosted by his part in A River Runs Through It (1992) as the Presbyterian minister who finds a bond with his sons (Craig Sheffer and Brad Pitt) through fly-fishing. It provoked the Hollywood Reporter to observe that “he has one of his richest roles in years as their emotionally cut-off father”.

The film, directed by Robert Redford , came out at the same time as Picket Fences (1992-96) was launched. This time, Skerritt was playing a warm, loving father, Jimmy Brock, a small-town sheriff married to Jill (Kathy Baker), a psychiatrist, with three children, in Rome, Wisconsin. “We’re the ones with whom the audience might most relate to – because all these other folks are crazy!” he said.

The quirky and daring storylines included cows’ udders exploding, animal sacrifice and date rape and tackled taboo subjects such as euthanasia, abortion, incest and homophobia – groundbreaking for peak-time US television at the time.

Skerritt’s performance won him a Primetime Emmy award as outstanding lead actor in a drama series and he was kept firmly in the public eye during the programme’s four runs. “I’ve never really been comfortable with celebrity,” he said, while admitting that Jimmy Brock was another role he had initially turned down before being won over by the storylines. When the series ended, he returned to guest roles on TV and supporting parts in films in a hard-working career in which he portrayed almost 200 screen characters.

Skerritt was born in Detroit, Michigan , to Roy Skerritt, a business executive, and his wife, Helen (nee Maybee). On leaving Mackenzie high school, he served in the US air force as a classification specialist (1951-55) before studying English, first at Wayne State University, then at UCLA (the University of California Los Angeles), where he took up acting. The director Denis Sanders and his brother, the producer Terry Sanders, spotted Skerritt in a stage production of The Rainmaker and cast him as a soldier in War Hunt (1962), alongside Redford.

Dozens of one-off TV roles followed such as My Three Sons (in 1963), Wagon Train (in 1964) and The Fugitive (two parts, in 1966 and 1967) before his appearance in M*A*S*H meant he was switching between the big and small screens.

He was a motorcycle cop in the film Harold and Maude (1971), choosing to be credited as Martin Bormann (the name of Hitler’s private secretary). “We did silly things in those days,” he explained.

Skerritt then played Shelley Duvall ’s father, a mechanic, in Thieves Like Us (1974), reuniting him with Altman; Shirley Maclaine’s husband, a retired ballet dancer, in The Turning Point (1977); a Vietnam veteran in the cult classic Up in Smoke (1978), alongside Cheech Marin and Tommy Chong; and Sally Field’s good-hearted husband, also the father of Julia Roberts, in Steel Magnolias (1989).

On TV, he was Kirstie Alley’s suave former boss, Evan Drake, in the sixth series of Cheers (1987-88), Joe Kennedy in Jackie Bouvier Kennedy Onassis (2000) and General William Westmoreland in Path to War (2002). He played Field’s husband again, this time deceased and appearing in flashback, in the first three series of Brothers & Sisters (2006-09).

Skerritt’s first two marriages ended in divorce. He is survived by his third wife, Julie (nee Tokashiki), whom he married in 1998, and their daughter, Emi, as well as by Andy, Dan and Erin, the children of his first marriage, to Charlotte Shanks, and Colin, the son from the second, to Sue Oran.

article_text:
This year the Editions sector brings together 48 publishers and specialist booksellers. Located on the first floor along the walkways and in the Galerie Courbe of the Grand Palais, it offers a panorama of international photographic publishing, from contemporary publications to historical and rare books.

Alongside publishers such as MACK (London), Atelier EXB (Paris) and Aperture (New York), the 2026 edition welcomes newcomers including Gato Negro and Obsidiana (Mexico City), Palm* Studios (London) and Sun Archive (Wrocław), as well as Fw:Books (Netherlands).

Throughout the fair, publishers host more than 400 book-signing sessions at their booths, allowing the public to meet artists and authors around their publications.

article_text:
FIAPF’s decision to make A-list status official, with Tokyo among the 17 festivals named, is unlikely to change much about the event, according to the filmmaker leading its competition jury.

Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer , the director of “Bad Boy Bubby” and “Ten Canoes,” was asked at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival ’s jury press conference on Tuesday whether the classification mattered or was a redundant system.

“I think Tokyo has always been considered one of those festivals by most people who attend festivals. Tokyo was effectively an A festival. And so in that sense, I don’t think it makes a lot of difference,” de Heer said.

He allowed that the classification seems to be carrying more weight in determining the quality of films a festival can secure. “And so in that sense, it may help that it is officially now again A, but I don’t think it changes the festival so much,” de Heer said.

In March, FIAPF, the international federation of film producers’ associations, replaced its four-category accreditation system with a single list and designated 17 festivals as A-list, a term the industry had long used informally. They include Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Toronto, Busan, Shanghai, Cairo and Tokyo. Busan and Toronto made the list for the first time.

Korean producer Oh Jungwan, founder of Bom Film Productions (“The Foul King,” “A Tale of Two Sisters,” “A Bittersweet Life”), said de Heer’s answer covered it and that she was “not a film festival person.”

“So I don’t know what is A-list or not. So maybe probably A-list means good, so but as an audience, we’re not going to the festival because of their A-list or not. We just go to watch film and enjoy the feeling, the festival feeling,” Oh said.

Pressed by the journalist, who had hoped someone would call out a system that ranks some festivals above others, de Heer offered a final word: “It matters a great deal to some people, and not at all to others. And that is as it should be.”

The rest of the jury, Japanese actor Watanabe Makiko (“M/Other,” “Love Exposure,” “Tokyo Vice”), New York- and Tokyo-based producer Alex Lo of Cinema Inutile, whose credits include Jim Jarmusch’s Venice Golden Lion winner “Father Mother Sister Brother,” and Tokyo-based colorist Yov Moor (“The Taste of Things,” “Grand Tour”), did not weigh in on the question. The five-member panel will choose the Tokyo Grand Prix from 15 competition titles. The festival runs through Nov. 4.

De Heer was also asked about prospects for Australia-Japan co-productions. “It makes no sense for a Japanese film to shoot in Australia, it makes no sense for an Australian film to shoot in Japan. Europe is very good at doing co-productions only on a financial basis, really. Australia is not so good at that,” he said. Co-productions built on “a natural story where some things need to be shot in Japan, some things need to be shot in Australia” will always be possible, he added, “if the scripts come and if they are right.”

Lo, whose “Heads or Tails?” won best director at Tokyo last year, said producers in Europe, the U.S. and elsewhere “are increasingly seeking co-production opportunities,” largely because local government support is lacking.

On how a divided jury would settle on a winner, de Heer said the answer would depend on the situation. “I’m with four other very reasonable people, and I’m sure we can find a way through that we don’t end up with some sort of lesser compromised film, but a really interesting film that maybe some of us don’t like,” he said.

Oh, a Tokyo juror for the second time, recalled once arguing for seven hours on behalf of a film. “Every other jury [member] hated me,” Oh said, adding that she hoped she would not have to fight de Heer for seven hours this time.

article_text:
The Film Independent Spirit Awards are returning to the Hollywood Palladium with a new pair of hosts in tow.

Film Independent, the nonprofit organization dedicated to championing independent storytelling and supporting artists, announced on Wednesday, December 10 that “ Maddie’s Secret ” stars Kate Berlant and John Early will co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards .

The acclaimed comedians, actors and longtime creative collaborators, who have written and/or starred together in other projects like Emmy-nominated variety special “Would It Kill You to Laugh?,” and cult comedy series “Search Party” will bring their comedic sensibilities to the 42nd annual Spirit Awards. The celebration of the best in independent film and television takes place Saturday, March 6, 2027 in Los Angeles, California.

“If there’s one thing we don’t need, it’s another predictable awards show,” said Juan Devis , President of Film Independent, as part of the announcement. “Kate and John are two of the funniest, strangest and most brilliantly unpredictable performers working today. They embody everything we love about independent storytelling: originality, fearlessness and a healthy disregard for convention. We’re excited to shake things up, break a few rules and have some fun along the way.”

“We’ve always been obsessed with awards shows, and we’re so honored we get to host the coolest one,” the hosts said in a joint statement. “Tune in to see if we choke under pressure!”

Nominations will be announced on Wednesday, December 2. The 2027 ceremony will introduce the Best International First Feature and Digital Creator Award categories , said to further expand the Spirit Awards’ recognition of bold, original storytelling across platforms and around the world.

In other recent developments, acclaimed filmmaker Roman Coppola will contribute to the ceremony in his new creative consultant role. The Nominee Brunch, an annual highlight honoring all nominees and featuring the presentation of the Emerging Filmmaker Awards, will take place on Saturday, January 9, 2027 at The London West Hollywood.

Berlant and Early join a roster of past Spirit Awards hosts that includes Ego Nwodim, Aidy Bryant, Hasan Minhaj, Megan Mullally and Nick Offerman, Aubrey Plaza, Nick Kroll and John Mulaney, Kate McKinnon and Kumail Nanjiani, Fred Armisen and Kristen Bell, Andy Samberg, and John Waters.

Familism）成長下的價值，以支持香港來到今日──當然如果投機行事下的「若有所成」，如同戲中父親留下賽馬獎金，讓女兒無意發現，就會是錦上添花了。 不過，女兒回應「我呢啲唔係叫嫁唔出，係呢個世界嘅男人娶唔入！」想到最近有大學教授的「釣金龜」言論，都由女主角之口當頭棒喝──後九七成長的世代，當然深明舊日價值有時如無稽之談，不過像戲中的父親可以嘻笑人生，那就可望之後的香港故事，或可被調侃作結。當然新生代能否如英文戲名「Good Trip」而也可以走一趟圓滿歷程，那就要看他們來到一條怎樣的公路矣。"}]

article_text:
Born in London in 1981, Natasha Bedingfield is a singer and songwriter. Her 2004 debut album, Unwritten, sold more than 2.3m copies and featured the No 1 single These Words. She has released three further albums, scoring UK Top 10 hits and success in the US with Pocketful of Sunshine. Nearly two decades after it was released, her single Unwritten became a viral TikTok hit in 2021. Her new single, Dot Dot Dot, is out now.

This was taken at Hilly Fields park in south -east London. I’m dressed in a sweet little tracksuit. I was a cute kid: I sucked my thumb until I was 11 and I had a sheepskin that I sniffed. But if anyone actually said I was cute, I’d reply: “No, I’m not!” I wanted to be taken seriously. That word made me think that nobody was listening to what I had to say.

My parents come from New Zealand, and when they had my brother Daniel they emigrated to England where they then had me and my two younger siblings. We lived in the inner city, so our backyard was a saviour. Together we were a pack and would spend all day making forts and watching frogs in the pond. We didn’t have much money, but I was rich in love.

I come from a family of big thinkers. My parents are social workers and raised us to believe that everyone is equal. We were taught that you should talk to everyone, as you never know when you could be standing in front of an angel. Mum and Dad wanted each of us to learn in our own way, outside of a system, so I was home-schooled from 11 until 16. Back then it was a rebellious thing to do, but I loved self-study. I am overwhelmed by loudness, so the fact I didn’t have to learn in a full class of students worked for me. It’s ironic, really, considering my profession, but too much noise makes me shut down. Is that a neurodiversity thing? Probably.

As well as my parent s’ outside -the -box approach , another big influence on my childhood was church. Every week we would go to a Jamaican church, one that really encouraged kids to get into music. I loved the culture there – as well as singing, we had a strong community of people of all ages.

When I was 18, I started travelling on the tube and doing late-night writing sessions with producers. My brother was the more obvious musician in the family. Daniel would be at home, saying things like, “Everyone be quiet – I’m recording!” Whereas I was more private – writing but keeping it to myself. Why? Some friendly acquaintances – family, friends – warned me that it might be hard to have two Bedingfields in the industry. “It’s very rare that it would happen for both of you,” they’d say. So I decided to get on with it quietly. In the end I said to my brother: “I know this is your thing, but it’s actually my thing, too. And I’m not trying to take over from you.” He, of course, supported me entirely.

Around the same time, I started studying psychology at university. I found the whole process stressful – I often felt dizzy, and struggled to learn all of the names and dates. My dad ended up saying: “We all know that you’re a singer-songwriter – that is what you should be doing.” He was the one who encouraged me to leave university and I will be for ever grateful.

When I started out, my label told me that I was a pop artist. But I wasn’t Britney. I didn’t even know what pop meant at the time, because I wasn’t keeping an eye on the charts, I didn’t listen to the radio. Even as a teenager I never had boybands on my wall. I was a fan of Coldplay, Björk, India Arie and Stevie Wonder. I didn’t want to mime, or pole dance. I was just trying to be authentic. The only time I did learn a dance routine was for the video for Single. I did a few moves, then felt weird. They wanted to make me sexy, but the whole thing looked forced. It was frustrating. Female artists often get boiled down to how we look and it takes away from the substance of what we’re actually saying.

I wrote Unwritten for my younger brother. It started as a poem, and then I tried to make it into a song with other writers, but they wanted to take a different approach, to do the whole blond bombshell pop type of thing. Then I met Danielle Brisebois [from New Radicals] and together we clicked and made Unwritten. The whole process felt simple. I wasn’t showing off vocally. I was just singing to my brother. I didn’t think about whether it would be a hit.

after newsletter promotion

After the success of my first album, I started taking myself less seriously in my lyrics. I’d grown into my humour, which is where a song like I Wanna Have Your Babies comes from. The track was restricted by BBC Radio 2 as they thought it was encouraging young people to have kids. But, really, it was meant to make people laugh as it was about the thoughts you never say out loud when you are dating someone new. In the end, my label sent me to the US – a way to test out my career without other parts of the world watching. They essentially geo-blocked me. I had hits in the US, but they were not released in England. I even sang at the White House for Obama, and my mum couldn’t watch it. It was a bit like being banished. The only bonus was that being a Briton in the US meant I could get away with certain things. Because I taught myself to read, there were some words I knew how to write but not say out loud. In my song These Words, I use the word hyperbole. A word I had never said out loud before. I sang it wrong for a long time, but told the Americans that was how you pronounced it in England.

After that I left my label and had a 10-year period where I was doing a lot of corporate shows and touring. I got married, had a baby and kept on songwriting. I wrote with some Swedish songwriters, but the songs didn’t show much growth. Then around the pandemic, people started making up dances to Unwritten. It went viral and I started having a resurgence. Some friends called and said: “Natasha, you have to become part of the conversation.” I didn’t get it at first. I thought TikTok was just a dance app and I didn’t want to dance. But once I saw the videos I realised it was a creative place to be. I’ve embraced the song’s new life ever since.

My goal now is to write my Purple Rain. I haven’t written my best songs yet and I want a timeless classic. Getting older doesn’t threaten me – artists like Tina Turner had careers that took off when they were my age. I find that so inspiring, as so often it’s, like, women are written off when they reach a certain age.

I still feel so alive when I am making songs. It’s that buzz of expressing an emotion that everyone feels, but is hard to articulate without music. I don’t get excited about the things other people do – I don’t like going to Disneyland or holiday resorts. Even on my birthday I would rather be in a recording studio, making songs and geeking out about a triple entendre, than at a party. I don’t think that will ever change.

article_text:
The American Film Market, or AFM , has long been the venue where independent films can find homes with international distributors, where packages can come together, and where producers and sales agents can mingle and take meetings. It’s an essential event on the calendar for many in the indie film world . Callo, meanwhile, is an operating system and platform that aims to bring that experience online, allowing independent creators to match up with producers, other collaborators, or studios.

It’s only fitting, then, that this year’s AFM will combine real-world interaction with the online connections to rethink how people network, connect, and collaborate at the market. It’s just the latest sign of how the market seems to be evolving under new IFTA president Jackie Brenneman .

IndieWire can share exclusively that Callo is the official collaboration platform for AFM 2026, which means that AFM participants will be given access to the Callo platform and can better find those people, projects, and opportunities they want to discover on the ground in Los Angeles before, after, or during the market. Badge holders can request access to Callo, and those creators who join can use it to find collaborators, build and package projects, review teams and materials, share film slates with potential partners. Likewise, it’s a useful tool for buyers, financiers, sales agents, and other executives to scope out new projects and talent.

AFM will also give Platinum badge holders special access to the service, including Callo’s intelligent matching and human curation. They’ll be invited to one-on-one meetings at a dedicated lounge at the Fairmont Century Plaza, and other participants will be hand-picked to receive a one-year membership to Callo Slate, a premium offering that offers other development, project management, and curation support year-round.

Additionally, Brenneman will also participate on a panel discussion along with Callo’s founder and CEO Fassa Sar, as well as Monica Khan, Founder & CEO of Creator Revolution and Senior Advisor to McKinsey & Company. The panel is titled “More Than a Trend: The Rise of Creator Filmmakers,” and it will touch on how the likes of Curry Barker, Kane Parsons, and Markiplier who have clear, established audiences online have managed to bring their work to Hollywood and the movie theater, something that has already sparked a gold rush of people trying to find the next online IP or talent discovery . The panel takes place on the AFM Main Stage on Wednesday, November 11 at 4:30 pm PT.

“It’s clear the marketplace is changing rapidly. The people entering film and television today don’t necessarily look like the people who built the industry before them. We’re seeing creators with audiences enter for the first time, alongside a new generation of producers, financiers, and creative entrepreneurs who looking to be real players in our industry,” Sar said in a statement. “Callo serves this new generation, giving them the infrastructure to develop projects, build teams, operate slates, and bring projects to market. That’s why partnering with AFM felt obvious. AFM has always been where the independent marketplace comes together to buy and sell. We see an opportunity to extend that ecosystem and give more people a way to participate, connect, and launch what they’re building at AFM”

“The rules and business models that have long defined our industry are being reinvented, creating new ways for projects to be developed, financed and brought to audiences. At the same time, this is still an industry built on relationships, and bringing the industry together has always been fundamental to AFM. We’re excited to partner with Callo to give our community a smarter way to discover the people and opportunities most relevant to them, make valuable connections and create new possibilities for collaboration and business,” Brenneman added in a statement.

AFM’s theme for 2026 is The New Global Screen Economy, and the market will have an expanded focus on the convergence of independent film and television, creators, technology, and new business models across development, financing, production and distribution at its inaugural Summit on opening day, November 10. It also introduced an AI track for AI startups as part of what will be called the AFM House and Innovation Hub.

AFM 2026 takes place November 10-15 at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles.

article_text:
Artist Tony Berlant has died at 85, reports the Los Angeles Times . L.A. Louver, his longtime gallery, confirmed the death.

Berlant, who was associated with the West Coast Pop art movement of the 1960s, was best known for large-scale collages made of shards of printed metal and thousands of nails. He often worked with vintage metal signs and occasionally added found objects to his pieces. In recent years, he had begun printing personal photographs onto the collages’ metal grounds, adding an autobiographical dimension to the works.

Berlant was born in New York City in 1941 and moved with his family to LA when he was five. After graduating from the University of California, Los Angeles in 1961, he went on earn master’s degrees in painting and sculpture in 1962 and 1963. His Pop-inflected works from the early ’60s featured real clothing painted with enamel and glued to canvases; by 1964, however, Berlant had moved on to his signature material, collaging pieces of found metal signage onto flat surfaces and three-dimensional shapes such as houses and cubes.

These works gained him early attention; between 1962 and 1966, Berlant was included in exhibitions at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, the Whitney Museum in New York, and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. He began showing with L.A. Louver in 1984.

In addition to his art practice, Berlant was a collector of Native American art and artifacts, an interest that grew to include Mimbres pottery from southwestern New Mexico (he was a founding member of the Mimbres Foundation, a conservancy group) and prehistoric stone tools. His books First Sculpture: Handaxe to Figure Stone (Nasher Sculpture Center), coauthored with anthropologist Thomas Wynn, and Decoding Mimbres Painting: Ancient Ceramics of the American Southwest (Prestel), written in collaboration with Evan Maurer and Julia Burtenshaw, were both published in 2018.

Berlant lived in Santa Monica, California. He is survived by his wife, performance artist and set designer Helen Méndez; his daughter, comedian and actress Kate Berlant; and a brother, Jeff Berlant.
